articles.text: David Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont Park on the 4th of July this year immediately following the parade. The concert show will begin at approximately11:30 a.m. on a large stage in the park on Monday, July 4 One of San Francisco’s premier party bands for 25 years, this “interactive” 11-piece allstar group has gained a national reputation for their high energy performances, incredible musical variety, and “anything can happen” hi-jinx. Recent appearances include The Waldorf Astoria in New York City, special Napa Valley performances for Wine Spectator Magazine, concertizing in Maui at the Hyatt Regency Kaanapali and La Costa Resort in Carlsbad; selling out in Reno at the Grand Sierra Resort’s VIP New Years Eve 2010; and entertaining at numerous benefit galas in the greater Bay Area. David Martin is a Bay Area native who began his musical career at the age of six. Known for his powerful vocals and sparkling guitar work, David was a founding member of legendary San Francisco “New Wave” faces The LLoyds and The Buzztones. articles.text: Origins of Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade In 2000, Piedmont lost Dick Johnson, the city’s beloved banjo-playing founder of the 4th of July Parade. As chairman of the Piedmont Recreation Commission in 1965, the man everyone called Pear decided to start a parade. In the early 1960’s under the leadership of neighbors Mary Ellen Sherry, Dorothy Carter and Carolyn Bostrom Renton, a block party was established to keep the children entertained on Independence Day. Events included bike decoration and a parade, a watermelon-eating contest, Professor Arthur Sherry reading the Declaration of Independence, a bar-bque, and swimming at 1504 Oakland Avenue. The concept of creating a citywide parade was pure Pear. “He said it was too quiet in Piedmont in the summer, and something needed to be done”, recalled close friend Ed Bartlett. “Pear came up with the idea of a parade. I told him it would never work – everybody’s at Tahoe. It took off right away. That’s the Dick Johnson plays his banjo with the Yerba Buena Jazz Band in the 1970s. kind of person Pear was.” Johnson was highly regarded for his prodigious musical talent. He wrote, produced, directed and performed in dozens of shows at The Family Club, Claremont Country Club and the Athenian-Niles Club. Every year on the 4th of July, his Yerba Buena Jazz Band rode by on the back of a truck, putting smiles on faces everywhere. The legacy of Dick Johnson is being carried out by his daughter, Kathy Kelleher, who is a member of the July 4th Parade Committee.

articles.text: The July 4 Parade Committee chose a patriotic theme for this year’s event: “Remember Why it’s the Fourth of July.” It’s a theme with intention, explained committee member Roland Lazzarotto. “I think that it is a suggestion that we look back at history and remember why we celebrate July 4 and Independence. We seem to be somewhat divided now as a country with political factions taking extreme views on the constitution and amendments. We may even see a former president convicted of numerous crimes. Yet the country will move on,” Lazzarotto explained. Lazzarotto, who serves as the parade’s official starter at the corner of Highland and Park Way, confirmed that the theme generates more discussion each year than any other item being considered by the 10-member committee. “We review themes from the past 20 years. We try to have a theme that will inspire neighborhood groups to enter a float and have something to build on,” he said. “A theme that has potential to be interpreted in multiple ways is a plus. This theme asks a question and that forces everyone to answer the question in their own mind.” Lazzarotto explained that the committee “tries to avoid the obvious political theme” but wanted to remain topical. “We like a theme that rolls off the tongue when spoken. We narrow it down to 3 or 4 then there is some lobbying on the part of committee members who really like one theme over another. In the end it is a consensus,” he said. The July 4 parade, the largest public event in the city, returns in full-force this Monday starting at 11 a.m. on Highland Avenue.
articles.title: 4th of July Parade theme: “Remember Why it’s the Fourth of July”

After my six years and retiring in Berkeley, I thought I would never be back to do this again. But there is no other place I would want to be than here. So, I thank you for this opportunity, and even though it is just a year, it will be a great year,” said Evans. W h e n R a n d y B o o ke r announced his resignation as Piedmont Superintendent in late Spring, School Board President Cory Smegal and board member Amal Smith spoke with the California School Board Association (CSBA) for advice on the best way to search for a new superintendent. They were advised Dr. Donald Evans, Piedmont School District’s newly named interim Superintendent, was introduced to the School Board on June 22. to issue a Request for Proposal (RFP) and use a search firm. Smegal and Board Vice President Megan Pillsbury spoke with several search firms and the district’s legal advisors and were told they could pursue the following options: 1) Use a search firm starting in late May and into the summer to try and have a Superintendent in place before school starts in August 2) Appoint an internal candidate as Interim Superintendent 3) Appoint an external candidate as Interim Superintendent “The board discussed these options and we agreed that doing a search starting in late May over the summer would not be in the district’s best interest,” said Smegal. “It would not provide enough time or availability for community engagement. Parents, teachers and staff who we would like to be involved in this process deserve a break this summer. It was going to be tricky to pull this off over the summertime,” Smegal added.

articles.text: The artificial turf at Becker Field at Havens Elementary School is in the process of being replaced. The process of pulling up the old turf began on Wednesday June 22 and installation is expected to be completed by the week of July 18. The new turf will cost Piedmont School District approximately $298,000, Director of Facilities Pete Palmer said the new Fieldturf product has a warranty of 7-10 years. Originally installed in 2010, the field was named after Piedmont resident Mark Becker who designed the new Havens School. At the time, Havens was the only elementary school without immediate access to a grass field. The previous turf consisted of artificial turf laid over a coconut husk infill and drainage mat. The composition kept the field easy to maintain, at a moderate temperate and soft for active kids. The expected life span of that turf was 6-8 years, but it has been in use for 12 years. The new surface will have an infill of natural cork and sand, similar to Witter Field. The field is used for many P.E. activities, by Piedmont Soccer Club, and when Witter Field floods, for high school practices. Parents at Havens raised nearly 10% of the cost of the field, and families contributing $1,000 or more, were given the opportunity to have their names “creatively displayed” around the field. “A big thank you must go out to Havens parents club for raising approximately $25,000 in donations to help pay for the new turf,” said Palmer. In the second week of construction, on Monday June 27, the Fieldturf at Becker Playfield at Havens School is removed and replaced by a new surface.

articles.text: Sally Ride Club Teen Volunteers “Do you weep when things go wrong on the job?” asked an interviewer before her first space flight, “Will the flight affect your reproductive organs?” Dr. Sally Ride was the youngest American to go to space, the first American woman in space, and the first known LGBTQ+ astronaut. For the Galaxy Explorers, student volunteers at Chabot Space and Science Center, her accomplishments are memorialized in the eponymous LGBTQ+ project team: Sally Ride Club. Her legacy is unmistakable. Yet her whole life, people waited for her to fail. Ride was born in 1951, a time when women’s career options were limited. However, Ride’s tennis prowess gave her access to scholarships for school and even introduced her to her future partner of 27 years, Dr. Tamara O’Shaughnessy. Ultimately, Ride gave up a potential career as a professional tennis player to follow what she loved: science. When NASA opened up their selection to women for the first time in 1978, Ride applied as a doctoral candidate at Stanford. She ultimately became one of the five female candidates selected, and she began her astronaut training the same year she received her PhD in astrophysics. Five years of NASA training and ground crew positions later, she boarded the Challenger and was hailed as the first American woman in space. As the expert with the shuttle’s robotic arm, she helped launch crucial satellites into orbit. Five months after her first mission she returned Sally Ride and Tam O’Shaughnessy with their dog, Gypsy, in 1992. for a second mission to continue her work. However, following the 1986 Challenger disaster, Ride’s third flight was put on hold and she instead served on the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. Later, she retired from NASA to teach and uplift women in STEM. After she came back to the ground from her second mission, Ride also fell in love with Tamara O’Shaughnessy, a doctor in school psychology. Ride and O’Shaughnessy were strong advocates of science, writing children’s books together and founding Sally Ride Science to encourage girls in STEM. It was only after Ride’s death that it was revealed that they also had a successful and long-lasting relationship together. Ride was able to rise up despite the obstacles of sexism. She was a brave and powerful force that changed the way that women in science were perceived, and she also made history as the first LGBTQ+ astronaut. Most people did not realize Ride was a lesbian until her obituary in 2012 revealed that she had been with O’Shaughnessy for 27 years. Chabot Space and Science Center’s Galaxy Explorers honor her story and keep her name alive with Sally Ride Club, an LGBTQ+ club and project team. Sally Ride Club is dedicated to making STEM more inclusive, in honor of Ride and for all LGBTQ+ trailblazers. She may have been unable to come out in her lifetime, but today Dr. Sally Ride is recognized as a true LGBTQ+ icon. Chabot Space and Science Center, is located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. You can check out the list of Chabot Space and Science Center clubs at the following link: Galaxy Explorers – Chabot Space Times. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 7 SUMMER THOUGHTS Why we’re called Sally Ride Club By Anabel Loucks and Chabot Sally Ride Club Teen Volunteers “Do you weep when things go wrong on the job?” asked an interviewer before her first space flight, “Will the flight affect your reproductive organs?” Dr. Sally Ride was the youngest American to go to space, the first American woman in space, and the first known LGBTQ+ astronaut. For the Galaxy Explorers, student volunteers at Chabot Space and Science Center, her accomplishments are memorialized in the eponymous LGBTQ+ project team: Sally Ride Club. Her legacy is unmistakable. Yet her whole life, people waited for her to fail. Ride was born in 1951, a time when women’s career options were limited. However, Ride’s tennis prowess gave her access to scholarships for school and even introduced her to her future partner of 27 years, Dr. Tamara O’Shaughnessy. Ultimately, Ride gave up a potential career as a professional tennis player to follow what she loved: science. When NASA opened up their selection to women for the first time in 1978, Ride applied as a doctoral candidate at Stanford. She ultimately became one of the five female candidates selected, and she began her astronaut training the same year she received her PhD in astrophysics. Five years of NASA training and ground crew positions later, she boarded the Challenger and was hailed as the first American woman in space. As the expert with the shuttle’s robotic arm, she helped launch crucial satellites into orbit. Five months after her first mission she returned Sally Ride and Tam O’Shaughnessy with their dog, Gypsy, in 1992. for a second mission to continue her work. However, following the 1986 Challenger disaster, Ride’s third flight was put on hold and she instead served on the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. Later, she retired from NASA to teach and uplift women in STEM. After she came back to the ground from her second mission, Ride also fell in love with Tamara O’Shaughnessy, a doctor in school psychology. Ride and O’Shaughnessy were strong advocates of science, writing children’s books together and founding Sally Ride Science to encourage girls in STEM. It was only after Ride’s death that it was revealed that they also had a successful and long-lasting relationship together. Ride was able to rise up despite the obstacles of sexism. She was a brave and powerful force that changed the way that women in science were perceived, and she also made history as the first LGBTQ+ astronaut. Most people did not realize Ride was a lesbian until her obituary in 2012 revealed that she had been with O’Shaughnessy for 27 years. Chabot Space and Science Center’s Galaxy Explorers honor her story and keep her name alive with Sally Ride Club, an LGBTQ+ club and project team. Sally Ride Club is dedicated to making STEM more inclusive, in honor of Ride and for all LGBTQ+ trailblazers. She may have been unable to come out in her lifetime, but today Dr. Sally Ride is recognized as a true LGBTQ+ icon. Chabot Space and Science Center, is located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. You can check out the list of Chabot Space and Science Center clubs at the following link: Galaxy Explorers – Chabot Space Times. Becker Field turf being replaced By Jay Russell The artificial turf at Becker Field at Havens Elementary School is in the process of being replaced. articles.text: The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s Ensemble group embarked on its first international tour in two years due to the worldwide pandemic. On June 14, the students boarded a plane in San Francisco and after a 24-hour travel day, arrived in Frankfurt, Germany. The group of 50 students, choral directors and chaperones experienced some travel woes, including airport delays and a long bus ride, but arrived safely in Herning, Denmark on June 16. During their stay in Denmark, the students visited Deep Forest Art Land, owned by Dorte Bille, conductor of the Midtvest Junior Choir. The open-air art center is defined as “Skovsnogen,” a space “that unfolds under the open sky.” On the fourth day of their journey the choir serenaded the Mayor of Ikast, Denmark, Ib Lauristen, as well as the student body of The International School. The Ensemble group prepared for their major concert in Herning at Valgmenighedskirke, a church Singers enjoy a summer day at Deep Forest Art Land, art center in Kibaek, Denmark. This exhibition is “Skovsnogen” – a space not defined by walls or ceiling but that unfolds under the open sky. Artistic Director Eric Tuan (center) speaks to the students before boarding a double-decker bus from Germany to Denmark. Charlotte Rowan, director of Herning Kirkes Drengekor (Boy’s Chorus) with Eric Tuan, Artistic Director of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. with stunning acoustics. articles.text: Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit received two pins from the California Highway Patrol for recovering stolen cars. Petit has been a police officer in Piedmont for four years. The awards are known as the Gold Pin. To be eligible an officer, during a 12-month period, must meet one of the following criteria: 1) Make six arrests in separate incidents of rolling stolen vehicles. 2) Recover a total of 12 stolen vehicles 3) Develop information resulting in the identification of a vehicle theft ring, make subsequent arrests of two or more suspects, and recover at least 10 vehicles. Piedmont police are alerted to stolen vehicles from the automatic license plate reader (ALPR) system. Verifying the legitimacy of license plates can also be done on readers located inside patrol cars. “The dispatcher will tell where it was stolen, if it was a carjacking or a strong-arm crime, and whether a gun was involved,” said Petit. Petit said he has gained a lot of knowledge about what is involved Piedmont Police Sergeant Robert Jaime (left) and Captain Chris Monahan with Officer Tyler Petit after he was awarded two pins by the California Highway Patrol. when pulling over a stolen car. “As far as anxiety goes, you just adapt to it because you do it so often. It is something you are mentally prepared for,” said Petit. The weekly log commonly shows as many as 15 ALPR triggers per week, most of which are stolen vehicles. The system can also be triggered by a stolen plate. “It has become the trend. These guys know cities are using the license plate technology so they get around it by switching the license plates [from a car on the street],” explained Petit. Some people believe that cameras are an invasion of privacy, but Petit sees them as less intrusive than tracking devices in every phone or modern vehicle. “Police officers aren’t sitting there all day waiting for [residents] to come home and eat dinner with [their] kids. We are waiting for that felony vehicle to enter a town we try to keep as safe as possible and either prevent them from coming in or try to capture them if we can,” said Petit. articles.text: Provided is a recap of five Piedmont baseball teams that competed in the 32nd Annual Millbrae Baseball Tournament Friday through Sunday, June 24-26. On Friday night, the Bulldogs lost 26-5 to the heavy-hitting Peninsula Pumas, but rallied to win the tournament. The Bulldogs bounced back on Saturday with a 21-7 win over the Pacifica Sea Dogs 21-7. In Sunday’s playoff bracket they defeated the No. 4 Sea Dogs 19-6 in the quarterfinals and won the semifinals with a 10-7 in victory over the South City All Stars. Once in the championship game on Sunday, they rolled past the San Bruno Gold, 7-1. The Bulldogs were led by the infield defense of Nicolas Bivens at short stop, Clive Alanis at third base, Teddy Dietrick at PA, Arian Singh at second base, Max Carver against the Millbrae Blue. They went on to play the Millbrae Gold team in the semi-finals, eventually losing 8-3. 11 & Under Piedmont Tigers The Tigers entered Millbrae looking to become three-peat champions after winning the title at the 8U and 10U levels. He will now face France’s Richard Gasquet on Thursday, June 30, in the second round. Mackie McDonald lifts his first after defeating Nuno Borges in the first round of the Wimbledon on Tuesday. McDonald was initially scheduled to play the tournament’s No. 14 seeded Marin Čilić, but the Croatian was forced to withdraw after testing positive for COVID-19. This opened the door for McDonald, No. 55 on the ATP ladder, to face the world’s No. 123 ranked Borges. Mackie was solid against Borges, recording 10 aces and was able to land 72 percent of his first serves. He took two of five break points as the receiver, totaling 32 points. He had a very strong two sets, starting both the first and second with a 4-2 advantage after stealing two games as the returner in both sets from the Portuguese. In the third and final set, McDonald and Borges traded points as the server all the way to 6-6, forcing a seven-point tiebreaker. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, June 29, 2022 Sports 5 Piedmont squads compete in Millbrae Baseball Tournament Provided is a recap of five Piedmont baseball teams that competed in the 32nd Annual Millbrae Baseball Tournament Friday through Sunday, June 24-26. Piedmont Baseball Foundation had one championship win, two other championship appearances, and another semifinals berth. 8 & Under Piedmont Bulldogs The Piedmont Bulldogs Overlay team traveled to Millbrae to compete in the Silver Division. On Friday night, the Bulldogs lost 26-5 to the heavy-hitting Peninsula Pumas, but rallied to win the tournament. The Bulldogs bounced back on Saturday with a 21-7 win over the Pacifica Sea Dogs 21-7. In Sunday’s playoff bracket they defeated the No. 4 Sea Dogs 19-6 in the quarterfinals and won the semifinals with a 10-7 in victory over the South City All Stars. Once in the championship game on Sunday, they rolled past the San Bruno Gold, 7-1. The Bulldogs were led by the infield defense of Nicolas Bivens at short stop, Clive Alanis at third base, Teddy Dietrick at PA, Arian Singh at second base, Max Carver against the Millbrae Blue. Next up for the Wildcats is the Foster City tournament beginning July 5. 10 & Under Piedmont Panthers The Piedmont Panthers played four games and overcame two losses in the pool stage. In the playoffs, they defeated No. 3 seed Millbrae Blue in an exciting 8-7 battle in the first round. They went on to play the Millbrae Gold team in the semi-finals, eventually losing 8-3. 11 & Under Piedmont Tigers The Tigers entered Millbrae looking to become three-peat champions after winning the title at the 8U and 10U levels. Wednesday, June 29, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. LUKE HARRIS Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Carleton College Class of 2025 Luke Harris just finished his freshman year at Carleton College in Minnesota as an AllMIAC selection after becoming a starter for the Knights. He finished last season with 710 total minutes played, shooting 47 percent from the field and converting 17 of 46 three-point attempts. He finished with 283 points, 72 assists, 21 steals, and five blocks. The Posy named Harris its 2021 Athlete of the Year following his senior campaign at Piedmont High. He finished his high school career with over 1,200 points, concluding the pandemic shortened 2021 season with 383 points, a sparkling 55 percent shooting, 85 free throws made, 46 assists, and 33 steals. A three-year starter at Piedmont, he’s part of three highly successful years. The team posted a 21-11 record in his sophomore season. He was the leading scorer on the North Coast Section championship team that had a school record 24-6 season. What is your workout program this summer? I am doing shooting workouts and open gyms at the high school 3 times a week, then plyometrics and weightlifting on the days in between What are your fitness goals for this summer? My fitness goals for the summer are to get in great cardiovascular shape while still maintaining the muscle that I put on during the school year. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by my ability to run for long periods of time, and trying to increase the duration week by week. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am doing shooting workouts with my dad, and I am working with a basketball trainer other days. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I received honorable mention all-conference and all first year team at Carleton this past year. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Don’t let anyone else determine the outcome of your athletic career except yourself. Make sure that your work ethic matches your goals. articles.text: A preview of this year’s course and favorite riders This year’s Tour de France marks the 109th edition of La Grande Boucle, starting with Friday, July 1’s Grand Départ in Copenhagen, Denmark. The world’s best known cycling race finishes at the Champs-Élysées in Paris on Sunday, July 24, after 3,328 kilometers of racing. This year is the first time the race has begun in Denmark. It is considered a long time coming for the Danes, given that Copenhagen is considered one of the world’s best cycling cities and the country has approximately 12,000 kilometers of bike routes. The city was set to host last year’s Grand Départ, but it moved to France due to COVID related scheduling conflicts. Denmark will host the first three days of the tour, beginning with a 13-kilometer (8.1 miles) time trial through Copenhagen followed by two flat stages, including a 199-kilometer ride from Roskilde to Nyborg in Stage 2 and 182 kilometers in Stage 3 from Vejle to Sønderborg. After a rest day, the Tour turns up the intensity without a flat course for nine consecutive stages. That could be a catalyst toward Tadej Pogačar winning his third consecutive tour. Stages 4-6 provides a collective 327 kilometers of hill riding, including 19.4 kilometers of Stage 5 featuring a cobblestone path that could contribute to crashes. Stage 6 starts in Binche, Belgium. The next stage is the first mountain course from France’s Tomblaine to La Planche des Belles Filles, providing 176 kilometers on the first summit finish of this year’s event. Stage 8 is a medium-mountain stage, 184 kilometers from Dole to Lausanne, Switzerland, the fourth different country in this year’s tour. Stage 9 features a climb into the Alps for 183 kilometers from Aigle, Switzerland to Châtel, France. Stage 10 is a medium-mountain 148-kilometer course that ends with a 19.2-kilometer summit finish at Megève. Stage 11 is a difficult 149-kilometer mountain course from Albertville to Col du Granon, with two steep ascents before a summit finish on the Col du Granon. Stage 12 is on France’s Independence Day, Bastille Day, July 14, providing a 166-kilometer mountain course and an exuberant celebration throughout France. The next four stages fluctuate from flat to medium-mountain runs before the final two mountain stages on 17 and 18. Stage 18’s 143-kilometer course features a final 13.6 kilometers of ascent to Hautacam, it will be the last chance for climbers to gain time. Stage 19 is a 189-kilometer flat course, Stage 20 a 40-kilometer time trial, and Stage 21 is the final day’s 112-kilometer ride into Paris to the ChampsÉlysées. It’s worth mentioning that Mark Cavendish, 37, won’t be in the running after failing to earn a spot on Quick-Step Alpha Vinyl Team. Last year he tied Eddie Merckx’s all-time record of 34 stage victories. Provided are the top five riders to watch. articles.text: Try the Post’s favorites 4 hikes at Lake Tahoe The Rubicon Trail provides a view of Lake Tahoe’s Fannette Island in Emerald Bay at Lake Tahoe. four trails at Lake Tahoe. Hiking season has arrived with summer and it’s the perfect time to get out and explore nature’s beauties. Lake Tahoe is always a frequent location for Bay Area families to enjoy the great outdoors and the refreshing mountain water. The location provides some of my favorite trails in the entire state, which we’ve been fortunate enough to hike and photograph. Here are the Post’s favorite 1. Horsetail Falls In Twin Bridges, between Strawberry and the Sierra-atTahoe Resort along Highway 50, you can see a magnificent 500- foot waterfall cascading down Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from the Stateline area. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip with 1,341 feet in elevation gain. While hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek, the trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks. Sturdy hiking boots are recommended. If hikers opt against making it all the way to the falls, there are countless areas where you can jump into the creek or merely sunbathe on the rocks. Beneath the falls is a popular swimming hole with ample space to jump, swim, or just wade. On a hot summer day, a dip into the cold water was the perfect refresher before the hike back down. The entire trail is largely unmaintained, but keeping your eyes on the main path was simple enough. There are also small blue-spray painted markings to keep hikers on the trail. Punch in “Pyramid Creek Trailhead” to access the parking lot, which is $10 for all day and overnight. 2. Rubicon Trail The Rubicon Trail is 5.9 miles out and back (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation. It stretches around Emerald Bay with a view of Fannette Island. Hikers can visit the historic Vikingsholm mansion on the island and nearby quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp, with countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. The trail travels beside the white sandy beach along Emerald Bay to the northern portion of the Rubicon Trail. The northern section of the Emerald Bay gives visitors a much more private look of Fannette Island, with spots along the shoreline to cool off on a hot day. One mile from Vikingsholm is the Emerald Bay Boat Camp, a secluded $30 per night boat-in campground. Less than one mile from the Emerald Bay Boat Camp entrance is the secluded Secret Cove, where you will see shallow crystal blue water. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré On any given Friday or Saturday night in the early 1960s, it was not unusual to pull into a drive-in filled with cars and kids, some leaning against fenders, others deep in conversation, and hear on more than one car radio Wolfman Jack, rock & roll DJ extraordinaire, a legend in his own time. “Let’s git nakkid” he’d call out as he segued into “It’s All Right (Mama)” by Elvis Presley, one of the first and perhaps greatest rock & roll songs ever. Wolfman Jack. Gravelly voice. Diabolical laugh. No one had ever seen him. He was an enigma. Rumor had it that he was on some ship off the coast of Mexico, staying one record spin ahead of the culture cops. Or possibly he was hold up in a beachside, cinderblock shack with a monster antenna, south of Tijuana. And, as it turned out, that’s exactly where the Wolfman was, slammin’ and jammin’ at station XERB-AM, sending out a powerhouse signal to all places north, up the coast of California, reaching Alaska on a clear night. What was undisputed was that the discs Wolfman played captured the essence of being young during the late 50s and early 60s. Rock & roll was transcendent. It was heart wrenching, spine-tingling, drop to your knees wonderful. And more. There was Big Joe Turner’s “Shake, Rattle & Roll” and Bill Haley and the Comet’s “Rock Around the Clock,” all precursors of some of the most vital, Motown inspired music to ever come out of the 50s, soon morphing into the Stones, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, James Brown and the Beach Boys. Rock & roll was the cresting wave, a cultural zeitgeist. Great Britain, in so many ways, mirrored America, creating it’s own unique version of rock & roll, led by groups such as the Who, the Kinks, Cream, Pink Floyd and, of course, the Beatles. And for a time, in the 60s, British kids tuned in late at night to a rogue rock & roll station, beamed from a ship somewhere off the coast. And that is the essence of the film Pirate Radio. An improbable group of disc jockeys kept rock & roll on the radio 24/7, to the absolute delight of the nation’s listeners and to the consternation of the British government and the BBC, which took great umbrage at the airways being filled with such “rot.” Led by Cultural Minister Alistair Dormandy (Kenneth Branagh), a concerted effort is set in motion to sink the renegade ship, so to speak, and shut down the illicit music once and for all. Rock & roll, it was decided, posed a threat to homeland security. Meanwhile, on board, the DJs are running a floating animal house, engaging in pranks and fun and music. The housemother, so to speak, is Quentin (Bill Nighy), the captain and titular head of this ragged crew, with The Count (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and Gavin (Rhys Ifans) filling the prime time radio slots. While the story is thin – there is a subplot, a sort of coming of age saga about young Carl, the nephew of Quentin – the energy and sheer delight conveyed by the film makes for sweet entertainment and the sound track, meaning the platters spun, is, simply, top drawer. Pirate Radio. Directed by Richard Curtis. Starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, Bill Nighy, Rhys Ifans, Talulah Riley and Tom Sturridge. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Pirate Radio – Wolfman Jack and the growth of rock & roll

Pirate Radio – Wolfman Jack and the growth of rock & roll Review by Chris Honoré On any given Friday or Saturday night in the early 1960s, it was not unusual to pull into a drive-in filled with cars and kids, some leaning against fenders, others deep in conversation, and hear on more than one car radio Wolfman Jack, rock & roll DJ extraordinaire, a legend in his own time. “Let’s git nakkid” he’d call out as he segued into “It’s All Right (Mama)” by Elvis Presley, one of the first and perhaps greatest rock & roll songs ever. Wolfman Jack. Gravelly voice. Diabolical laugh. No one had ever seen him. He was an enigma. Rumor had it that he was on some ship off the coast of Mexico, staying one record spin ahead of the culture cops. Or possibly he was hold up in a beachside, cinderblock shack with a monster antenna, south of Tijuana. And, as it turned out, that’s exactly where the Wolfman was, slammin’ and jammin’ at station XERB-AM, sending out a powerhouse signal to all places north, up the coast of California, reaching Alaska on a clear night. What was undisputed was that the discs Wolfman played captured the essence of being young during the late 50s and early 60s. Rock & roll was transcendent. It was heart wrenching, spine-tingling, drop to your knees wonderful. And more. There was Big Joe Turner’s “Shake, Rattle & Roll” and Bill Haley and the Comet’s “Rock Around the Clock,” all precursors of some of the most vital, Motown inspired music to ever come out of the 50s, soon morphing into the Stones, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, James Brown and the Beach Boys. Rock & roll was the cresting wave, a cultural zeitgeist. Great Britain, in so many ways, mirrored America, creating it’s own unique version of rock & roll, led by groups such as the Who, the Kinks, Cream, Pink Floyd and, of course, the Beatles. And for a time, in the 60s, British kids tuned in late at night to a rogue rock & roll station, beamed from a ship somewhere off the coast. And that is the essence of the film Pirate Radio. An improbable group of disc jockeys kept rock & roll on the radio 24/7, to the absolute delight of the nation’s listeners and to the consternation of the British government and the BBC, which took great umbrage at the airways being filled with such “rot.” Led by Cultural Minister Alistair Dormandy (Kenneth Branagh), a concerted effort is set in motion to sink the renegade ship, so to speak, and shut down the illicit music once and for all. Rock & roll, it was decided, posed a threat to homeland security. Meanwhile, on board, the DJs are running a floating animal house, engaging in pranks and fun and music. The housemother, so to speak, is Quentin (Bill Nighy), the captain and titular head of this ragged crew, with The Count (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and Gavin (Rhys Ifans) filling the prime time radio slots. While the story is thin – there is a subplot, a sort of coming of age saga about young Carl, the nephew of Quentin – the energy and sheer delight conveyed by the film makes for sweet entertainment and the sound track, meaning the platters spun, is, simply, top drawer. Pirate Radio. Directed by Richard Curtis. Starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, Bill Nighy, Rhys Ifans, Talulah Riley and Tom Sturridge. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated R. Democracy is not a spectator sport! articles.text: It’s evident going in that Tomb Raider will be a B-movie (pulp cinema). As well, it’s a 2018 reboot of the 2001 Lara Croft: Tomb Raider (starring Angelina Jolie). For good measure, that earlier film was based on a video game, not a comic book. Recall that B-films, when good (and some are really good), represent a special niche in Hollywood. They are the films that that give definition to the term cliffhanger, and prepared the way for contemporary action films, which are derivative of the old Republic Films serials featured in matinees on countless Saturdays. Kids filled the balconies, hands sticky with Milk Duds or JuJubes, sitting stone still when Don Winslow of the Navy careened off a cliff in a black town car (with massive whitewalls). They groaned when the screen was suddenly filled with “To Be Continued.” I don’t think it’s a stretch to point out that the Aquaman in The Shape of Water could be the twin of the man-fish in the 1950s film, The Creature From the Black Lagoon. Ditto the pulpy sci-fi films of the same era, B-movies all. Tomb Raider is remarkable, and as tightly put together as is Alicia Vikander, portraying Lara, who’s completely buff and totally up to what proves to be a fast-paced series of cliffhangers requiring serious physical challenges. It’s pedal to the medal, even in the opening backstory scenes. For seven years, Lara has been grieving for her father, Lord Richard Croft (Dominic West), refusing to believe he is dead. He vanished during an expedition. However he does leave Lara with a clue, discovered as she sits in one of his corporate offices, preparing to sign a document that will do two things: acknowledge he is deceased, thus making her officially the heir to a massive fortune. Clue in hand, Lara abruptly leaves the conference room and returns to the Croft estate, a place she has not visited since his disappearance. She has refused to use his wealth or live in what is actually her home. In his crypt she discovers a secret room, filled with research and a journal that explains where Alicia Vikander stars as Lora Croft in Tomb Raider. he has gone, warning her not to follow; instead she is instructed to burn his papers. Apparently, her father was in the hunt for the tomb of a demonic queen, buried in a mountain on an island in what is known as the Devil’s Triangle, off the coast of Japan. Cut to Hong Kong where Lara is looking for a specific rusty freighter and passage to the Triangle and then to the island shown in his journal. Thus begins the Lara Croft adventure, heading into the unknown, with a drunken captain (David Wu), no crew, and a map. It’s at this point it becomes evident that the story is clearly derivative of The Raiders of the Lost Ark, an iconic adventure film that has inspired not only sequels, but other A/B movies. As an aside, Lara is no Wonder Woman and is never portrayed as a superhero. Nor is she the fragile wife in The Danish Girl (which earned her an Oscar). She is vulnerable while being incredibly courageous and brave and willing to risk all as she searches for her father. Of course, despite treacherous seas and the rusty ship breaking up on the rocks off the found island, she perseveres. What happens is part of the fun of this well-crafted movie – nicely told and gorgeously made. Know that Vikander invests fully in the character. She delivers a fearless performance and is supremely athletic. She is also supported by a talented ensemble of fine actors. The villains are, well, dependably villainous, led by Walter Googins as Mathias Vogel, a man obsessed, even after seven years, with finding a way to break into the forbidden tomb. This is flat-out good B-movie making. And if you’re a fan of this genre, then don’t miss Tomb Raider. Tomb Raider. Directed by Roar Uthaug. Starring Alicia Vikander, Dominic West, Walton Goggins. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

Review by Chris Honoré When filmgoers sit down to watch an apocalyptic movie, it’s a given that they suspend their disbelief regarding all that is outlandish. They simply sit back and enjoy the ride. And what a ride it can be. With the ever-growing sophistication of special effects (CGI), films of this ilk grow ever more dramatic and intense. Consider 2012, released in that same year. It’s “end of times” filmmaking on steroids. King Kong of catastrophe. The movie followa a familiar template. Act one: ivory tower scientists, usually reserved in their discourse, discover that a serious problem is approaching, one that could have a devastating impact on the planet and mankind. Act two: how to sell the data to recalcitrant and even hostile government officials. With the help of seismic events – earthquakes, hail showers at the equator, volcanoes erupting, temperatures fluctuating dangerously – the officials are brought around. The question then is, what to do to prepare for the event. Act three: the protagonists find themselves in harm’s way as the crisis escalates and they struggle to survive. All around them, destruction is occurring on a scale never seen before. Act four: the climax and denouement. The sun rises, but on a completely changed world. All of the central characters have survived – bloodied, exhausted, but still standing. Again, not enough can be said regarding the role played by CGI in constructing these films. The technology has taken movies such as this to a totally different realm. The narrative is important, but these movies are rarely about unresolved relationships. Small problems are solved (“Do you really love this guy?”), while trapped in a ship’s compartment with water flooding in, the rising water being far more important than the answer to the question. To create this film, 1,000 people worked at 15 different special effects studios to create the nonstop catastrophes, to include a blue screen that was 600 feet long and 40 feet high. The movie is endlessly gripping and the crises are stacked like Legos with few moments of relief. There will be those who say that John Cusack, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Amanda Peet and Oliver Platt, all exceptional actors, are wasted on this type of movie, given the flat dialogue and skinny plot. But it’s a given that both exist in service of the action – what’s ahead, what’s behind, and how can we save ourselves. As armageddon films go, 2012 is a solid example. One other note: Hollywood has been very successful in creating post-apocalyptic films. An event has occurred, something that has changed the earth dramatically (a worldwide epidemic, a war). How often, in the set-up to such a film, does the central character emerge to find mankind gone, the streets empty, cars abandoned, stores empty. The challenge is, how to survive. Examples would be The Postman, Planet of the Apes, I Am Legend, and The Omega Man. Survival is again the theme. Adapting to a world after a cataclysm is a far different proposition, though no less interesting. 2012. Directed by Roland Emerich, Starring John Cusack, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Amanda Peet, Oliver Platt and Woody Harrelson. 2 hrs., 53 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: There is a lot more to life than the headlines. Everyone knows the name William Randolph Hearst. And why not? He had a very public persona. There is, of course, the castle. And then, there were the sensational parties as well as various and sundry affairs. Need I go on? A chance meeting with the great grandson of William Randolph Hearst resulted in an invitation to a banquet. As I spoke with WR Hearst’s distant relative, I realized that he is about as good a host as was his great grandfather. He explained that there is much more to the Hearst story than the castle itself. WR Hearst always referred to the castle as “the ranch”. And that ranch completely surrounds the imposing castle. He also reminded me that there was much to be appreciated in the largesse of great grandpa. Aside from the gift of the castle itself, there has been a tremendous amount of money given to education and scholarships. The sumptuous banquet I attended featured beef from the Hearst ranchlands that go from the hilltop down to the ocean at San Simeon. The banquet also had two kinds of red wine, also from the Hearst ranch. For some time I have been rather disappointed by the quality of beef available in the stores. It is both tough and tasteless. But, wonder of wonders, the beef from the Hearst cattle ranch was so tender it was easy to cut with a fork. In flavor, it was ideal. The younger Hearst told me that his cattle are grass fed and grass finished. No wonder the Hearst beef is so good and why other beef is so bad. It was the same story with the wines. articles.text: Voodoo and Hoodoo cast spells using a mojo charm bag to ward off evil spirts and for healing. A mojo bag may include herbs, minerals, feathers, animal parts, animal and human bones. Hoodoo is an African diaspora folk magic occult tradition created during slavery in the United States. It is unique to black people. The Voodoo spiritual system combines Christianity, Islam and Black Spiritualist religions. Voodoo is a group of religions in the Americas, including Brazilian Vodum, Cuban Vodú and Santeria, Dominican Vudú, Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo and New Orleans Voodoo. From New Orleans to Chicago especially there is a thread of African America blues songs that embody field hollers, work songs and spirituals in a minor key, usually based on the minor pentatonic scale and on a single chord. They are chant-like, dark and mysterious. They use a musical mojo bag of catchy phrases. Such songs are Howlin’ Wolf’s Spoonful, Smokestack Lightning and Back Door Man; Muddy Waters’ Mannish Boy, and I’m Your Hootchie Kootchie Man. Mojo Voodoo Blues is in this style. Muddy Waters’ 1957 song Got My Mojo Working referred to the magical powers of a mojo bag. Hoodoo Man Blues is the notable debut album by blues vocalist and harmonica player Junior Wells, performing with the Junior Wells Chicago Blues Band, an early collaboration with guitarist Buddy Guy. Screamin’ Jay Hawkins’ I Put a Spell On You is an outrageous supernatural experience, inspired by Hoodoo (with guitarist Mikey Baker who wrote The Complete Course in Jazz Guitar). Popular “mojo” songs by black artists include Mojo Mama by Wilson Pickett, Mojo Handby by Little Buster & the Soul Brothers, Mojo Hannah by the Neville Brothers and Fiesta Mojo by Muddy Waters wrote Got My Mojo Working in 1957. Dizzy Gillespie. Popular “Voodoo” songs include Voodoo Child by Jimi Hendrix, Voodoo by the Neville Brothers, Voodoo by Shay Lia, Under My Voodoo by Sublime, Black Magic Woman by Peter Green and by Santana, and Voodoo Woman by Koko Taylor. Listen to and read my improvised example for this Mojo Voodoo Blues column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. The repetitive chord progression to Mojo Voodoo Blues is E-A-G-E, as you can hear repeatedly in the intro. The melodies are largely vocal-oriented melodies in the field holler style. The notes “B” and “D” are frequently used (the last two notes in bar 10), sounding an E7 chord. The mood is darkened with “Bb” the flat five of the key in bars 22-29. Bars 31-35 , 47-50 and 53-57 feature an interplay between the low and high range of pitch, suggesting two instruments. Memorize much or all of the piece and begin using fragments of it in building your own improvisation. Fun! Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: The Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, celebrates returning to live concerts this summer with three public performances at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening July 20. Festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind us that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jarmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), and Paul Laraia (viola). This Week’s Featured Artist: Jasmine Lin, Violin One of four musicians who has performed each year at the festival in Piedmont, Jasmine Line is a member of the Formosa Quartet with Deborah Pae and Festival founder Wayne Lee. “Jasmine Lin is a magnificent player with superb tone and strong interpretive powers” and “a violinist of remarkable intensity”, maintain American Record Guide and the Chicago Tribune. As a member of Formosa Quartet and Trio Voce, faculty member at Roosevelt University and Music Institute of Chicago, Curtis Institute of Music alumna, confidante to a Cremonese violin, arranger of Grappelli tunes, prizewinner in the Naumburg and Paganini competitions, Grammy nominee, Violinist Jasmine Lin returns to Piedmont for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. and recording artist on Con Brio, EMI, and New World Records, Jasmine likes to solicit magnificence and intensity while leaving raindrops on her nose un-wipedoff. Her biography contains precisely one hundred words. Tickets are $45, with a savings on season passes for all three concerts for $120. To reserve tickets now and for more information, including complete biographies of all musicians and details of the music program, visit the website: www.piedmontcmf.org. All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in Piedmont.

For a woman under age 25, getting birth-control pills, an increasingly costly prescription, costs her nothing; and for women over age 25, insurance pays 65%. She is required to participate in a counseling session where her pregnancy options are fully explored, followed by a period of reflection for at least 48 hours before she may return for a medical procedure. A pregnant female who is a minor under 18 years old retains rights relative to her body, personal health, and choice. France’s official policy is for every person to enjoy responsible, satisfying, and safe sex with the freedom to choose to have children, if, and when they wish. Recent polls show that opinions have grown more divided as to whether 220,000 yearly abortion procedures during the past two decades are an acceptable norm. The French public, like every western society, are swayed by national and foreign news reporting, and the array of infinite clicks leading to both informed and misinformed websites. The panoply of religious and political constructs is head-spinning, vying for your money and amassing more devotees. Pro-abortion and anti-abortion messaging bombards the Millennials (born 1981 to 1996) and Gen-Zees (born 1997 to 2012) to induct them into their orthodoxy. Activists, not just in France, but throughout Europe, the Americas, and especially in the United States, demand that embryos be given the same legal status as human beings. Russia, and former Communist countries offer abortion on demand in the first twelve weeks of gestation. Amnesty International has filed at their behest at the European Court of Human Rights, enjoined by eight other human rights agencies. Under Chancellor Olaf Scholz, Germany is proceeding on the promise to decriminalize abortion. Last Friday, the Bundestag parliament struck down the nearly century-old Nazi-era statute, according to Reuters. As recently as last year, clinic websites warned Google searchers that abortion could cause depression, trauma, and infertility, according to gynecologist Kristina Hänel, who was found guilty of “advertising” abortions under §219-a and led to a yearslong protest to effect modernization of Germany’s laws supporting women’s health. Especially in small towns, abortion is a taboo topic, and fearing a reputation as an aborNorth Wales Chronicle tion doctor, they demur. Possibly one in ten doctors provide abortions and considering the many rural areas and heavily Catholic state of Bavaria, medical practices have dwindled over the last two decades, falling by 40%, according to Deutsche Welle (DW) news service. In the documentary Scorned, Concealed, Prohibited, (Deutsche Welle (DW), viewers are introduced to Ordo Iuris, a self-described “very conservative Christian anti-choice think tank” and a European Humanist Federation whose quest is influencing European legislation through their considerable legal expertise. Unfortunately, these kinds of examples are relatively few. Far too much of the built world in which we live today is mediocre, uninspiring or even sometimes depressing. One-story strip malls line our roadways, old city centers deteriorate as big box retailers drive them to bankruptcy, and parking lots dominate the landscape. Why is this? articles.text: Yann Menager has for many years worked as the vineyard manager for the famous Yves Cuilleron winery in the Northern Rhone valley. Using knowledge he gained from that position, he has purchased some superbly sited vineyards to start producing tiny quantities of his own wines from those vineyards. He now produces wine from St. Joseph, Condrieu and Cote Rotie. He tries to keep his winemaking as simple as possible with a minimum of intervention. His production is small with just five to ten barrels of each wine produced each year. Very little of his wine makes it to the U.S. and we are lucky to have Jack Edwards an importer in Napa now bringing in his wines. His tiny winey is located in an old stone barn high above the vineyards of Saint Joseph on his family’s farm in the hamlet of Champailler. The vineyards are tended organically, picking is done by hand, yields are kept low, and he uses native yeast and natural malolactic conversion. The result is a range of wines that shows superb energy and balance, with a freshness and finesse that harks back to a day before super extraction and new oak became popular. These are beautifully fresh terroir-driven wines that speak of the soils in which they were grown. • 2019 Domainie de la Roche Paradis Condrieu Veauvignere Produced from a small 20-year-old Viognier vineyard near the medieval town of Malleval. Ginger, white pepper, and honeysuckle blossom all feature in this medium bodied wine, plus layers of apricots and melon emerging in support of a long, luxurious finish. Drink over the next five years. • 2019 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Saint-Joseph La Bergerie Blanc This is a blend of 50% Marsanne and 50% Roussanne planted on granite soils. Fresh, lively, crisp, and medium-bodied, it has classy notes of citrus blossom, herbs, and light minerality on the nose. Pure, elegant, and crystalline. Drink over the next five years. Perfect with oysters or other shellfish. Yann Menager works the vines. • 2019 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Saint-Joseph Les Vessettes 100% Syrah from 18-year-old vines planted on granite soil, the wine offers sumptuous notes of violets, black pepper, mint, and hints of black fruits. Elegant on the palate, with beautiful length and purity. This is a high-class wine. • 2018 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Cote-Rotie Rozier Made from 100% Syrah from the Rozier vineyard site, this is an elegant old-school style Cote-Rotie. It is loaded with gamy and meaty characteristics, as well as black currants, raspberries, tapenade and loads of peppery spice. Medium-bodied, layered and beautifully ripe, forget the bottles for 4-5 years and enjoy the following decade. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 23 The Wine Corner Domaine de la Roche Paradis – A gem of the Rhone By Pierre DuMont Yann Menager has for many years worked as the vineyard manager for the famous Yves Cuilleron winery in the Northern Rhone valley. Using knowledge he gained from that position, he has purchased some superbly sited vineyards to start producing tiny quantities of his own wines from those vineyards. He now produces wine from St. Joseph, Condrieu and Cote Rotie. He tries to keep his winemaking as simple as possible with a minimum of intervention. His production is small with just five to ten barrels of each wine produced each year. Very little of his wine makes it to the U.S. and we are lucky to have Jack Edwards an importer in Napa now bringing in his wines. His tiny winey is located in an old stone barn high above the vineyards of Saint Joseph on his family’s farm in the hamlet of Champailler. The vineyards are tended organically, picking is done by hand, yields are kept low, and he uses native yeast and natural malolactic conversion. The result is a range of wines that shows superb energy and balance, with a freshness and finesse that harks back to a day before super extraction and new oak became popular. These are beautifully fresh terroir-driven wines that speak of the soils in which they were grown. • 2019 Domainie de la Roche Paradis Condrieu Veauvignere Produced from a small 20-year-old Viognier vineyard near the medieval town of Malleval. The group was pleased to welcome first-time walker Linda Siegel, and Norene and Dan Stucka from Illinois visiting family. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group dodged another weather bullet last Wednesday. The day before had been in the 90s, but on June 22 it was a great morning, and 26 walkers showed up at the Exedra for a weekly walk. It had been almost three years since the group had walked the streets that were on the early 20th Century Key System streetcar lines, and a return to see them was overdue. Charlene Louie, who lives in a home on the former Key System No. 10 line, offered to lead the group on a tour of the area. In the 1890s the area that would become Piedmont was largely dairy farms and open space. As the East Bay population grew in the later years of the 1800’s, land developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate,” which acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay. Potential buyers needed transportation to get from their new homes to work in the area and in San Francisco. From its beginning, the Key System was conceived by Borax Smith as a way to sell The Realty Syndicate’s land. Borax Smith’s transportation system was a consolidation of several streetcar lines assembled in the late 1890s and early 1900s. After having made a fortune in borax mining in Nevada (hence his nickname) he and Havens turned to real estate and electric traction for streetcars. The Key System was founded as the San Francisco, Oakland, and San Jose Railway (SFOSJR), and incorporated in 1902. Service began in 1903 in Berkeley. In 1904 service started in what was to become the City of Piedmont. The Key System connected the East Bay to San Francisco by a pier on the Bay where passengers boarded a ferry to San Francisco. Later, after the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, Key System trains ran on the lower deck of the Bay Bridge, with the upper deck reserved for cars going both east and west. The electric streetcars replaced the cable car system in the East Bay, and soon Piedmont had three streetcar lines, the Numbers 10, 11, and 12. The No. 10 line traveled from downtown Oakland along Broadway to the Piedmont Avenue Key Route station at 41st Street, along Pleasant Valley and Grand Avenues through central Piedmont to the Hall Fenway at Crocker and Hampton. These streetcar lines made more neighborhoods in Piedmont desirable. Streetcar lines were routed to serve the real estate properties, thereby enhancing their value by offering convenient, efficient public transportation. In its early years, the Key System was actually a subsidiary of the Realty Syndicate, as was the Oakland-San Francisco ferry. Paths, lanes, walks and stairways were put in place in many of the newly developed neighborhoods, often in the middle of a city block, so that commuters could walk more directly to the new train system. The Key System ultimately provided mass transit in the cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Emeryville, Piedmont, San Leandro, Richmond, Albany, and El Cerrito from 1903 until 1960, when it was sold to a newly formed public agency, AC Transit. The local streetcars were discontinued and replaced by buses in 1948, and the commuter trains to San Francisco were discontinued in 1958. Charlene led the walkers on Highland Avenue to explore the lower portion of the former Number 10 route. The group came to Park Way where Highland is reduced from four lanes to two This is because at Park Way the train line turned off Highland and went down the hill, and over to Ramona and Arroyo Avenues. The walkers went down Park recognizing the construction of the older homes on the left side of the street and the newer mid-century homes on the right. The latter infill homes were built after the trains stopped running, and the Key System right of way land was made available for home construction. These homes have streets on both the front and back of the properties, with no backyard neighbors. Some homes have their front doors and addresses on Park Way, while other homes have theirs on Ramona. The walkers took the 107-foot path from Park up to Ramona where they were surprised to hear the clucking of chickens behind a resident’s wall. The group went down Ramona to Monticello

articles.text: We all want to live long lives. We all expect to live long lives. But are we financially prepared for this longevity? Before we get to the issue of preparation, let’s look at a couple of interesting findings from a 2022 survey by Age Wave and Edward Jones: 1. The surveyed retirees said, on average, they expect to live to 89, and they said the ideal length of retirement is 29 years. 2. When asked if they want to live to 100, nearly 70% of the respondents said “yes.” The main reason for this desire for long life? To spend more years with their family and friends. Of course, none of us can see into the future and know how long we’ll be around. But with advances in medical care and a greater awareness of healthy lifestyles, these aspirations have a real basis in reality. However, if you’re going to enjoy a longer lifespan, and the extra years with your loved ones, you need to ensure your finances are also in good shape. How can you make this happen? Here are some basic steps to follow: • • Save and invest early and often. This may be the oldest piece of financial advice, but it’s still valid. The earlier you start saving and investing for your retirement, the greater your potential accumulation. Consider this: If you began saving just $5,000 per year at age 25, and earned a hypothetical 6.5% annual rate of return, and didn’t take any early withdrawals, you’d end up with $935,000 by the time you reached 65. But if you waited until 35 to start saving and investing, and you earned the same hypothetical 6.5% return – again with no early withdrawals – you’d only end up with $460,000. And if you didn’t start saving until 45, you’d end up with just over $200,000, again given the same 6.5% return. Be mindful of debt. You may not want to be burdened with certain debts when you enter retirement. So, while you’re still working, try to reduce unwanted debts, particularly those that don’t offer the financial benefits of tax-deductible interest payments. The lower your debt load, the more you can save and invest for the future.
articles.title: Prepare yourself for a long retirement

articles.text: Searching for the wizard of OGG. The airline flew us to a mystery Pacific island they designate as OGG, far out to sea, close enough to the Equator that the North Star looks merely like the night firmament’s belly-button, splashed by the sea swell. The airline provided a oncea-lifetime surprise in mid-air, donating a glass of chardonnay on learning of my 90th, celebrated days before. Moral: I recommend that every one work to turn 90, and frequently, to let the airline continue its largesse. OGG, weird name and all, is no recent discovery, to judge by the hundreds of hotels dotting its shores and beaches amongst the big black lava rocks, decorated here and there by U.S. flags. The locals were happily bilingual, speaking both English and US currency. Hard-belching volcanoes had come and gone, spewing lava over thousands of eruptions by grace of the fire-god Pele, enough to produce peaks near 10,000 ft., and land enough that any island circumnavigation by car takes more than an hour. Palms abound, requiring machete-wielding aerialists to shinny up the 40-foot trees to chop off weighty palm fronds before they attack you on windy days. If one broke off, I’d hope to be hit by the soft external fringes in descent. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 25 Prepare yourself for a long retirement We all want to live long lives. We all expect to live long lives. But are we financially prepared for this longevity? Before we get to the issue of preparation, let’s look at a couple of interesting findings from a 2022 survey by Age Wave and Edward Jones: 1. The surveyed retirees said, on average, they expect to live to 89, and they said the ideal length of retirement is 29 years. 2. When asked if they want to live to 100, nearly 70% of the respondents said “yes.” The main reason for this desire for long life? To spend more years with their family and friends. Of course, none of us can see into the future and know how long we’ll be around. But with advances in medical care and a greater awareness of healthy lifestyles, these aspirations have a real basis in reality. However, if you’re going to enjoy a longer lifespan, and the extra years with your loved ones, you need to ensure your finances are also in good shape. How can you make this happen? Here are some basic steps to follow: • • Save and invest early and often. This may be the oldest piece of financial advice, but it’s still valid. The earlier you start saving and investing for your retirement, the greater your potential accumulation. Consider this: If you began saving just $5,000 per year at age 25, and earned a hypothetical 6.5% annual rate of return, and didn’t take any early withdrawals, you’d end up with $935,000 by the time you reached 65. But if you waited until 35 to start saving and investing, and you earned the same hypothetical 6.5% return – again with no early withdrawals – you’d only end up with $460,000. And if you didn’t start saving until 45, you’d end up with just over $200,000, again given the same 6.5% return. Be mindful of debt. You may not want to be burdened with certain debts when you enter retirement. So, while you’re still working, try to reduce unwanted debts, particularly those that don’t offer the financial benefits of tax-deductible interest payments. The lower your debt load, the more you can save and invest for the future. • Keep reviewing your progress. It’s important to monitor the progress you need to make toward achieving your goal of a comfortable retirement. Over the short term, your investment balances may fluctuate, especially in volatile financial markets such as we’ve seen in the early part of this year. But you’ll get a clearer picture of your situation if you look at long-term results. For example, have your accounts grown over the past 10 years as much as you had planned? And going forward, do you think you’re in good shape, or will you need to make some changes to your investment strategy? Keep in mind that, if you’re 50 or older, you can make “catch-up” contributions to your IRA and 401(k) that allow you to exceed the regular limits. You may also want to adjust your investment mix as you near retirement to potentially lower your risk exposure. Hopefully, you will enjoy many years of a healthy, happy retirement. And you can help support this vision by carefully considering your financial moves and making the ones that are right for you. articles.text: As an adult son or daughter, spouse, or even grandchild, you want to help a loved one when they become ill, or their abilities change as the result of natural aging. But are there some things that you would prefer a professional caregiver do instead? Let’s get real: not everyone is prepared to bathe their loved one or discuss potentially embarrassing topics. Have you found yourself in one of these predicaments? 1. You notice that a loved one doesn’t smell the same. A change in a person’s odor can be a sign of illness so the first step is to schedule an appointment with their health care provider for a check-up. They may also need to see a dentist, so add that to the checklist. Have they stopped bathing or showering? Are they changing their clothes? Has their diet changed? These are all things to investigate with as much kindness as possible and to get medical professionals involved; for support and so the advice comes from a trusted third-party. 2. Speaking of smells, how does their home smell? As senses dull due to aging or illness, a person’s ability to sniff out food that has gone bad or the need to take out the trash can become an issue. Is the solution to hire someone to help out with weekly housekeeping? Or can a caregiver add light housekeeping to their responsibilities when they come over for medication reminders? Having a clean and fresh-smelling environment might lift their spirits and provide something to look forward to consistently. 3. Back to that lapse in bathing…if you’re an adult daughter, for example, are you comfortable giving your elderly father a bath? There are many reasons why elderly people stop bathing themselves: fear of falling, symptoms of dementia that mean they forget the frequency or steps involved, inability to control water temperature, and more. Hiring a professional caregiver to take on this task is a good option, but then this person needs to be scheduled at a time that is best for your loved one for optimum results. 4. Your loved one won’t go out to eat with you or anyone else, or sit across the table from you to share a meal at home. It’s time for some delicate detective work so that they can once again partake in this pleasant shared activity with others, in part to decrease potential feelings of loneliness. Again, this might be a health problem that needs to be addressed by a dentist or their healthcare provider. If you’re eating with a loved one who is unable to keep their food and drink from spilling or ending up on their clothes, it’s time for some compassionate conversations to help them find a solution to the chewing and swallowing problems they are experiencing. 5. All of the above topics can mean it’s time to have “the talk” with your loved one. Often one of the first signs that someone’s ability to be completely independent shows up is in their driving. Even once you’ve practiced the conversation in front of a mirror, met with their healthcare provider, and done research on local longterm care options, this can be a very challenging talk for families and friends. Be prepared to listen, put yourself in their shoes, show respect, and be patient as they process their options such as home care services and using a caregiver. Becoming a family caregiver can happen gradually with a few errands and evolve into more personal care that requires training to do safely. Caregiving can also happen suddenly after an accident or illness such as a stroke, but the needs for personal and companion care might be the same and prove to be overwhelming for family and friends. Hiring a home care professional can be an act of true kindness in the face of an awkward situation, to preserve the relationship you both know and cherish. During this season, our residents’ lives are enriched by how close they live to this spectacular body of water, set right in the heart of the city. “It’s like we live right across the street from the lake,” laughs Sam. “Our building at Madison and Lakeshore Avenues is right on the lake and most apartment homes have either a water or city view,” he added. If Lake Merritt itself is getting a lot of attention these days, it’s because of the $198 improvement program for the lake that Oakland’s voters endorsed and was completed a few years ago. The 3.4 miles of sidewalks around the lake are smooth and easy to walk on, and every day the tides move into the lake. Because Lake Merritt is connected to the Bay and Pacific Ocean through the rebuilt Lake Merritt channel, fresh salt water comes into the lake twice a day. If the lake is truly at the heart of the city, then Damon Tighe is the rock star who sings its songs. Tighe, a frequent guest speaker at The Lake Merritt’s free Topics of Merritt program, is gathering quite a following for his frequent talks about what’s going on beneath Lake Merritt. Tighe works on biofuels and single cell genomics in the Bay Area and teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories. He has wonderful Damon Tighe explains exhibits to visitors. presentation skills. In March he made a presentation to The Lake Merritt about “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters.” There was a lot of excitement this spring as Chinook salmon were found in the lake for the first time in over 20 years. The salmon were working their way into the East Bay watershed to spawn. These fish and other creatures have come into the lake through the newly renovated tidal inflow area near the pedestrian bridge on the West side of the lake. Tighe also cited the dark and mysterious bat rays which are now visiting the lake. They can sometimes be spotted from shore, or at the bridge overlook. We also learned about a wide variety of smaller creatures, including some of the mollusk family who are Gloria Frey on Lake Merritt making their homes just under the water near the lake’s shores. Tighe also showed us the microscopic-sized visitors that are an important part of the immense diversity of the revitalized lake. I am a fan of the people who founded and continue to operate the non-profit Lake Merritt Institute. One of their important programs is enlisting volunteers to keep the lake clean. You can see these friendly folks around the lake with nets and poles, the tools that help them scoop out plastic bags and trash that has drifted into the lake. Since 1996, these intrepid volunteers and school groups have pulled out between 1,000 to 9,000 pounds of trash from the lake each month. The group also raised money and partnered with the City of Oakland to ensure that two largescale aerating fountains, situated directly in the lake, splash water high into the air, providing beauty and oxygen to what can sometimes be oxygen-poor water. We are lucky to have such a treasure in our midst. As summer gets going and you find yourself in need of a temperate breeze, or a little extra exercise, or a picnic site, visit Lake Merritt and enjoy one of the very best things about Oakland. articles.text: What grandparent doesn’t want to indulge their grandchildren? We want to buy them their wished-for birthday present, allow them to eat forbidden sweets, let them watch one more video that they’re begging for. And why shouldn’t we? After all, we’re grandparents! Haven’t we waited long enough for this? Lots of grandparents believe it is their right – no, their duty to spoil their grandchildren. It’s what everyone expects us to do. What possible harm could come from being spoiled by your grandparents? Authors Paul and Diana Miller write in A Guide to Great-Grandparenting (rev. 2021) that for one thing, the practice of spoiling one’s grandchildren contradicts and denigrates the good values, attitudes, and behaviors that parents are trying to instill in their children. Parents have enough difficulty agreeing on rules and expectations for the children they are raising together. It’s even tougher if the child has vastly different sets of rules at home than with their grandparents. The authors go on to describe the adverse long-lasting effects of spoiling: Spoiling is treating people in such a way that they develop a self-image of privilege, lack of self-discipline, lack of accountability for their actions, and are in general obnoxious. We all know people with these traits, and nobody enjoys being around them. It’s unlikely that any grandparent would want to feel that they contributed to the development of their grandchild’s personality and outlook on life in such a negative way. Why do grandparents spoil? Sometimes it’s a way to make up for the things they couldn’t give their own children when they were young. It could be that some grandparents feel a sense of insecurity that without special treats of every kind, children will not enjoy being in the company of the older adults and perhaps won’t love them. Many grandparents simply like to see their grandchild’s happy face. Others spoil children just because they have the means to do so. Alas, each new toy, game, or sweet is soon forgotten. A more meaningful way to indulge your grandchildren is by making sure that they always feel your unconditional love for them. When grandparents communicate to young children that they are loved just for being who they are, they feel secure and confident. Deeply loved children who feel accepted and treasured for themselves, and not for their accomplishments, their good looks, or their perfect behavior, grow into kind, generous, compassionate adults, who can be selfless and responsible.
