Haven’t we waited long enough for this? Lots of grandparents believe it is their right – no, their duty to spoil their grandchildren. It’s what everyone expects us to do. What possible harm could come from being spoiled by your grandparents? Authors Paul and Diana Miller write in A Guide to Great-GrandWhat’s wrong with spoiling my grandchildren? parenting (rev. 2021) that for one thing, the practice of spoiling one’s grandchildren contradicts and denigrates the good values, attitudes, and behaviors that parents are trying to instill in their children. Parents have enough difficulty agreeing on rules and expectations for the children they are raising together. It’s even tougher if the child has vastly different sets of rules at home than with their grandparents. The authors go on to describe the adverse long-lasting effects of spoiling: Spoiling is treating people in such a way that they develop a self-image of privilege, lack of self-discipline, lack of accountability for their actions, and are in general obnoxious. We all know people with these traits, and nobody enjoys being around them. It’s unlikely that any grandparent would want to feel that they contributed to the development of their grandchild’s personality and outlook on life in such a negative way. Why do grandparents spoil? Sometimes it’s a way to make up for the things they couldn’t give their own children when they were young. It could be that some grandparents feel a sense of insecurity that without special treats of every kind, children will not enjoy being in the company of the older adults and perhaps won’t love them. Many grandparents simply like to see their grandchild’s happy face. Others spoil children just because they have the means to do so. Alas, each new toy, game, or sweet is soon forgotten. A more meaningful way to indulge your grandchildren is by making sure that they always feel your unconditional love for them. When grandparents communicate to young children that they are loved just for being who they are, they feel secure and confident. Deeply loved children who feel accepted and treasured for themselves, and not for their accomplishments, their good looks, or their perfect behavior, grow into kind, generous, compassionate adults, who can be selfless and responsible. These are the kinds of children most grandparents are proud to watch grow up and delight in being around. So, go ahead, shower your grandchildren. With love. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Visitors learned about the history of the railroads, which played such an important role in the development of California. The idea of a railway museum started in 1946 when individuals learned that an old Oakland streetcar that they had chartered for a day’s outing was to be scrapped within a week. Railroad enthusiasts came up with enough money to buy the car on the spot. Dedicated railroaders wanted to preserve the old streetcars and they selected Solano County as the site. Their daunting task to transform 22 vacant acres into a living history museum, and in 1985 the Western Railway Museum was officially unveiled. The museum’s mission is to continue to preserve the regional heritage of electric railway transportation as a living resource for the benefit of present and future generations. The museum is run by dedicated volunteers and people interested in preserving the golden era of the trains. The Piedmont Seniors first took a one-hour train ride 11 miles from the museum. At the half-way spot, they got off the streetcar so that the seats could be placed in the reverse position for the return trip. Along the way they observed cows, horses, and jackrabbits, along the route, along with some scenic views of Mt. Diablo, and – from a distance – Mt. Tamalpais. The conductor was eager to explain the intricate workings of the train car, and his enthusiasm was contagious. After that the Seniors were in for a special treat. They had a fabulous docent, Bob, who had been giving tours for 40 years. His knowledge of East Bay history was amazing. Some were perfectly restored, and others were in their original condition waiting to be restored. One boxcar on display showed how hobos traveled unnoticed underneath the bottom of the train car, something that looked both dangerous and very uncomfortable (see photo). There were many photos of trains in the early 1940’s, including one of a train stopping at St. Mary’s College in Moraga for students, as well as a photo of the former train station in Lafayette. Imagine the Seniors’ surprise when they saw a photograph of the train that stopped at the corner of Highland and Oakland Avenues in Piedmont. The group learned about the history of the various train cars in the “Barn” and were told about the importance of the refrigerated train cars for transporting meat, fruit and vegetables, and the need for large quantities of ice to keep food from spoiling on long journeys from Chicago to Oakland. After observing the exterior of the trains, the group was allowed to go inside a decades old cabin car and a Pullman sleeper. They learned that the men’s bathrooms were much larger than the women’s because they needed room for their daily shaves. The sleeper cars were reminiscent of the berths from the movie Some Like it Hot. These cars catered to gentlemen who would take the trains from San Francisco to Los Angeles on business. The Pullman Company even hired dedicated employees who had to stay awake all night in case someone from the top bunk of a sleeper car needed to be escorted down the ladder to the restroom. The seniors noticed a baseball bat on the wall of the sleeper car, and asked if it was used for unruly passengers. No, they were told. It was used to crush ice to keep the rail cars cool. Lunchtime in the Delta were over, everyone was famished, so they headed to Rio Vista on the Sacramento River, a 15-minute drive, and had lunch at “The Point”, alongside the Delta. The views were very scenic with deck side seating outside. The food was well worth the wait, and it was relaxing to escape to a slower, laid-back town. You don’t have to be a train enthusiast to appreciate the Western Railway Museum. You just need to have appreciation for a slower time in America and an appreciation for a bygone era. Don’t miss the gift shop; it has gifts for children as well as adults and is fairly reasonably priced. The museum has a shaded area for picnics with a snack bar next to the museum. If you are looking for a short day trip, the Western Railway Museum is a wonderful excursion for people of all ages. The group meets monthly, usually on the fourth Wednesday of the month at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, at 10 a.m. beginning with refreshments and mingling, followed by a short meeting. The group also goes on monthly excursions to interesting destinations in the Bay Area. Seniors of all ages are welcome; you do not have to be a Piedmont resident to join. They are tasked with carrying out a crucial role in wildfire prevention, but for them, it’s more like five-star dining ‘alfresco.’ The herd was brought to the city to perform weed abatement by grazing on the hills surrounding the Corporation Yard and Coaches Field in Moraga Canyon. Using goats is an alternative to the use of herbicide and mowing, and is a resource that Piedmont has used for years. On Saturday, the goats went to work right away, eliminating dry grasses, weeds, and woody growth - all potential fire hazards.
